Culture.title: A Robbie Williams film starring a CGI chimp helped me come to terms with my hearing loss
Culture.summary: I was bullied for my deafness as a child, and just when I was finding myself, a car crash set me back years. But then I watched the movie Better Man, and had my life explained for me I cannot say I’ve ever been a Robbie Williams fan. When I went to see Better Man, the 2024 biopic in which Williams is played by a CGI chimp, I was tagging along with my wife. To be honest, I was sceptical about the ape but tried to meet the film with an open mind. I wasn’t looking for anything in particular but what I found was something that seemed to explain my life. I was born two months premature in Winnipeg, Canada, in 1961, with severe hearing loss in both ears that wasn’t diagnosed until I was seven. In 1969 we moved to Woking in Surrey; my father left and my mother descended into alcoholism. I was a misfit in my family, with no support for my deafness, and at school the bullying – from kids and teachers – was something awful. In my desperate isolation, I turned to reading: book reading, lip-reading, and reading the room. Forget TV, forget music – the Beano andBeezer were my survival manuals: the Numskulls taught me how my brain worked with broken ears. Continue reading...

Culture.title: Fontaines DC review – thrilling gothic grandeur from a band vaulting into greatness
Culture.summary: M&S Bank Arena, Liverpool Just a few years since playing little dive bars, the Irish rockers have confidently scaled up to huge rooms like this – and are now one of the key interpreters of modern malaise A mere seven years since their debut, Dogrel, Fontaines DC have enjoyed a virtually seamless passage from Dublin dive bars to arenas, with stadiums to follow next year. Each step has been taken seemingly effortlessly in their stride and this latest outing is no exception. Bathed in shimmering blue light, the band are well into hymnal opener Six Shot Morning before we even see sight of singer Grian Chatten. He wanders on while singing, an entrance worthy of Frank Sinatra. Chatten has previously seemed to distrust showbiz, but if anything the singer seems far more comfortable on the bigger stage than he ever did on smaller ones. With his Korn T-shirt, unfeasibly baggy trousers and tiny tattoo reading “deadly” in capitals, he leaps around, raises his arms to whip up the crowd and points the microphone towards them to sing key lines. Similarly, music this intense, dark, elegiac and even bleak – which speaks to the void at the heart of much modern life – is hardly typical arena fare but works brilliantly by taking on a more anthemic, celebratory aspect. It’s certainly weirdly thrilling hearing Chatten’s lines such as “We’re all depressed, running on a wheel” or “I don’t feel anything in the modern world” – or a song as plainly dark as Jackie Down the Line – become enormous, arena-uniting sing-songs. Continue reading...
